newsitem.title: JAPAN: Matsushita, on path to recovery, raises forecast.
newsitem.headline: Matsushita, on path to recovery, raises forecast.

text.p: Consumer electronics giant Matsushita Electric Industrial Co reported on Tuesday a surge in third-quarter profits, helped by high-tech products and a weak yen, and also made upbeat forecasts for the future.

Matsushita -- whose products are sold under the National, Panasonic and Technics brand names -- raised its full-year profit forecast once again, after an upward revision of business estimates only three months ago.
Clearly on the road to recovery, Matsushita also announced a sweeping measure to rid itself of bad loans made during the economic "bubble" to its troubled finance unit, NL Finance.
The bubble, a period of inflated asset prices, lasted from the late 1980s to the early 1990s.

Matsushita said it would write off long-term loans worth 100 billion yen ($819 million) to NL Finance in the current year, saying repayment from the unit was no longer expected at a time when real-estate prices continued to sag.
"The decision was made in response to the worsening environment in which NL Finance operates in order to collect its loans made to real-estate developers in Japan," Matsushita said in a statement.
Matsushita will take a special charge of 104 billion yen ($852 million) in parent-only results in the year to March 31, but said it would be offset by a special gain from stock sales.
Matsushita also plans to write off another 100 billion yen bad debt at NL Finance in the next business year and thereafter, it said.

For the October-December quarter of 1996, Matsushita's group net profit jumped 35 percent from a year earlier to 45.3 billion yen ($371 million), while operating profit surged 52 percent to 119.7 billion yen ($981 million). Sales rose 11 percent to 2.03 trillion yen ($16.6 billion).
Communication and industrial equipment sales continued to show strong growth, increasing 28 percent over a year earlier during the quarter, Matsushita said.

"Rapid expansion in mobile communication equipment sales, particularly cellular phones, was a major contributing factor to the growth," the company said in a statement. Sales of computer peripherals, such as hard-disk drives and personal computer displays, also advanced, it said.
The weak yen also helps Matsushita's overseas sales by reducing foreign currency-denominated sales prices.

Matsushita said it expects record group sales of 7.5 trillion yen ($61.4 billion) for the year to the end of March, up 10 percent from a year earlier. Last November it estimated group sales for the year at 7.4 trillion yen ($60.6 billion).
Group net profit is seen rising to 120 billion yen ($983 million), up 12 percent and up from a forecast in November of 115 billion yen ($942 million). (1$=122 yen)
